title: Rosemary's Baby (film)
wiki_lead:
Rosemary's Baby is a 1968 American supernatural psychological horror film written and directed by Roman Polanski, based on Ira Levin's 1967 novel. It stars Mia Farrow as Rosemary, a newlywed living in Manhattan who becomes pregnant, and begins to suspect that her elderly neighbors are Satanists who have sinister intentions regarding her and her baby. The film's supporting cast includes John Cassavetes, Ruth Gordon, Sidney Blackmer, Maurice Evans, Ralph Bellamy, Patsy Kelly, Angela Dorian, and Charles Grodin in his feature film debut.
Polanksi adapted the film's screenplay from Levin's novel, and the film was produced and partly-funded by William Castle, a producer known primarily for making low-budget horror films. It marked Polanski's first American production. Although the film is set in New York City, the majority of principal photography for Rosemary's Baby took place on soundstages at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles throughout late 1967. 
Rosemary's Baby had its world premiere on June 12, 1968, and went on to become the eighth highest-grossing film at the United States box office that year, grossing over $30 million. It was met with significant critical acclaim and received numerous accolades, including multiple Golden Globe Award nominations and two Academy Award nominations, winning Best Supporting Actress (for Ruth Gordon) and the Golden Globe in the same category. Internationally, Farrow was nominated for the BAFTA Award for Best Leading Actress, while the film won the award for Best Foreign Film from the French Syndicate of Cinema Critics.
Since its release, Rosemary's Baby has been widely regarded as one of the greatest horror films of all time, and in 2014 was selected for preservation in the United States National Film Registry by the Library of Congress as being "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant." Critics and film scholars in the intervening years have analyzed numerous themes in the film, including paranoia, women's liberation, Catholicism, and the occult. The film was followed by the 1976 television sequel Look What's Happened to Rosemary's Baby, a 2014 miniseries, and a 2024 prequel, Apartment 7A.

Plot
Guy and Rosemary Woodhouse rent a recently vacated apartment in the Bramford, a large Gothic building in Manhattan, after the previous tenant, an elderly woman, fell into a coma and died. Guy and Rosemary ignore their friend Hutch's warning about the Bramford's dark past involving witchcraft and murder. Rosemary meets a young woman, Terry Gionoffrio, a recovering drug addict whom Minnie and Roman Castevet, the Woodhouses' elderly next-door neighbors, took in. Rosemary admires a pendant necklace the Castevets gave to Terry but dislikes its pungent odor. One night, Terry apparently jumps to her death from the Castevets' seventh-floor apartment. Soon the Castevets befriend Guy and Rosemary. Guy grows increasingly fond of them, but Rosemary finds them annoying and meddlesome. Minnie gives Terry's "tannis root" pendant to Rosemary as a "good luck charm".
Guy lands an important role in a play after the original actor inexplicably goes blind. With his career on track, Guy wants to have a baby with Rosemary. On the night they plan to conceive, Minnie brings them individual cups of chocolate mousse. Guy chastises Rosemary for complaining hers tastes odd. Shortly after, Rosemary loses consciousness and experiences a dreamlike vision in which a demonic entity rapes her while Guy, the Castevets, and other Bramford tenants—all nude—watch. The next morning, Rosemary's body is covered in scratches. Guy admits to raping her while she was unconscious since he did not want to miss "baby night".
When Rosemary becomes pregnant, the Castevets insist she see their close friend Dr. Abraham Sapirstein, a prominent obstetrician, rather than her own physician, Dr. Hill. During her first trimester, Rosemary suffers severe abdominal pains and alarming weight loss. By Christmastime, Rosemary's gaunt appearance alarms Hutch, who begins researching the Bramford's history. The day she is to meet Hutch to discuss his findings, Rosemary is notified that Hutch has fallen into a coma. At a dinner party, Rosemary confesses her concern to her girlfriends. Later, she begins discarding the mysterious "health drinks" Minnie provides her. When Rosemary tells Guy she wishes to see Dr. Hill, he gets angry. As they argue, the pains suddenly stop and Rosemary feels the baby move for the first time.
Three months later, Hutch's friend Grace notifies Rosemary that Hutch has died. Just before his death, he asked Grace to give Rosemary a book on witchcraft along with the cryptic message: "The name is an anagram". Rosemary studies the book and deduces that "Roman Castevet" is an anagram for "Steven Marcato," the son of a former Bramford resident and a reputed Satanist. She suspects the Castevets belong to a Satanic coven and intend to sacrifice her baby. When she visits Saperstein to confess her fears, he assures her that Roman is in ill health and does not have much longer to live. Meanwhile, Guy discounts Rosemary's suspicions, leading her to fear he may be conspiring with the Castevets.
Rosemary conducts further research and learns that covens utilize personal items to perform spells. She recalls that Guy acquired a necktie of the actor he replaced shortly before he went blind. Convinced Guy has joined the coven, Rosemary packs her belongings and visits Sapirstein's office. She is alarmed when the office receptionist makes a casual comment about Sapirstein smelling of tannis root. Rosemary flees and visits Dr. Hill, who assumes she is delusional and calls Sapirstein, who arrives with Guy and takes her home. Rosemary locks herself in the apartment, but coven members infiltrate and restrain her. Sapirstein sedates a hysterical Rosemary, who goes into labor. When she awakens, she is told the baby was stillborn. As Rosemary recovers, she hears an infant crying, which Guy claims belongs to new tenants.
Believing her baby is alive, Rosemary examines a linen closet that shares a wall with the Castevets' apartment and discovers a hidden door connecting them. In the living room, the Castevets, Guy, Sapirstein and other coven members are gathered around a cradle. Peering inside the cradle, Rosemary is horrified to see that the child has the same eyes as the figure that raped her in her dream. It is revealed that the child was not conceived by Guy, but by Satan himself, and is destined to lead his followers in a spiritual revolt. In exchange for Guy's cooperation, he was gifted professional success. The coven begin exclaiming "Hail Satan" before a hysterical Rosemary. When Guy tries to calm her, Rosemary spits in his face. Roman gently urges her to be a mother to the child. Rosemary appears stunned, but after hearing the infant's cries, she tenderly begins to rock the cradle.

Themes


Women's autonomy
Writer Eleanor Johnson observes coercive control and domestic violence against women as prominent themes in the film, which she views as "one of the greatest horror films of all time" as well as "one of the most sociological." Johnson cites Guy's manipulation of Rosemary—coordinated with the Castevets—culminating in her rape by Satan and eventual birthing of the antichrist, as evidence of this: "Whatever supernatural horrors may arise in this film, there is a foundational domestic horror at work: Guy is a betrayer, a liar, and the facilitator of acute sexual violence toward his own wife. But as is too often the case in real-life instances of reproductive coercion, the reality is too horrible for Rosemary to hang onto, and she concludes, upon waking up, that it was, in fact, just a dream."
Scholar Brooke Coughenour comments that motherhood and pregnancy are "one side of the domestic themes" present in the film: "Rosemary’s rough pregnancy that she is made to believe is normal reflects a classic maternal anxiety: whether or not something is wrong with the baby."


Catholicism

Catholicism has been cited as a significant theme in the film, particularly Rosemary's lapsed faith, which renders her a susceptible target to the Satanic cabal seeking to use her as a vessel. Journalist and film critic Renata Adler described the film as a "seriously lapsed-Catholic fable." Nick Ripatrazone, writing for America magazine, describes the film as "intensely Catholic" and notes that it emphasizes aspects of Rosemary's Catholic guilt, specifically in the surreal dream sequence in which she is raped on the night of Pope Paul VI's visit in New York City: It is against this papal backdrop—and Guy’s curious narration of “Christ, what a mob”—that one of the most infamous scenes in the history of horror films unfolds. Rosemary collapses, and Guy carries her into bed, where she begins to have hallucinations. Despite her paltry defense of the church early in the film, Rosemary is God-haunted in her visions. She has already dreamt about an aggressive nun and now imagines being on a yacht with those most royal American Catholics, the Kennedys. One of her friends—a man who warned her about the apartment building’s Satanic past—is not allowed on the boat. “Catholics only,” she is told.
Scholar Thomas Aiello observes American "religious uncertainty" as "a function of social progress" as another theme. Aiello comments on a scene in which Rosemary reads an issue of Time magazine in Dr. Saperstein's office with the cover page reading "Is God Dead?", which was the magazine's actual April 8, 1966 cover story. Chicago Tribune journalist Norma Lee Browning observed that audiences would "look at the movie in different ways depending on their religion—or lack of it," feeling that the verity of the film's supernatural elements could be interpreted from multiple perspectives. 
Polanski himself felt that the novel was open to interpretation, and that the apparent supernatural events and existence of the coven could be viewed as a paranoid fantasy stemming from Rosemary's strenuous pregnancy. Farrow, however, commented that she took the events literally, stating: "I felt, when seeing the movie, that it wasn't in her mind." Farrow speculated that the reason the newborn Antichrist was not shown onscreen had to do budgetary restrictions, while Polanski commented in 2012 that he felt it would have been a "great mistake" to show the baby.


Production


Development
In Rosemary's Baby: A Retrospective, a featurette on the DVD release of the film, screenwriter/director Roman Polanski, Paramount Pictures executive Robert Evans, and production designer Richard Sylbert reminisce at length about the production. Evans recalled William Castle brought him the galley proofs of the book and asked him to purchase the film rights even before Random House published the book in April 1967. The studio head recognized the commercial potential of the project and agreed with the stipulation that Castle, who had a reputation for low-budget horror films, could produce but not direct the film adaptation. Castle ultimately provided $150,000 in funds to help make the film, and makes a cameo appearance as the man at the phone booth waiting for Rosemary to finish her call. 
François Truffaut said that Alfred Hitchcock was first offered the chance to direct the film but declined. Evans admired Polanski's European films, particularly Repulsion (1965), and hoped he could convince him to make his American debut with Rosemary's Baby. He knew the director was a ski buff who was anxious to make a film with the sport as its basis, so he sent him the script for Downhill Racer along with the galleys for Rosemary's Baby. Polanski read the latter book non-stop through the night and called Evans the following morning to tell him he thought Rosemary's Baby was the more interesting project, and would like the opportunity to write as well as direct it. grok_lead: Rosemary's Baby is a 1968 American psychological horror film written and directed by Roman Polanski, adapted from Ira Levin's 1967 novel of the same name. The story centers on Rosemary Woodhouse (Mia Farrow), a young New York City housewife whose pregnancy becomes entangled with sinister forces after she and her actor husband Guy (John Cassavetes) move into the Bramford, an ominous apartment building inhabited by eccentric elderly neighbors including the Castevets (Ruth Gordon and Sidney Blackmer). Produced by William Castle and released by Paramount Pictures on June 12, 1968, the film employs subtle dread, unreliable perceptions, and everyday settings to evoke paranoia about medical authority, spousal betrayal, and supernatural conspiracy. Critically praised for its atmospheric tension and Polanski's meticulous pacing, Rosemary's Baby holds an 8.0 rating on IMDb from over 250,000 user votes and 97% approval on Rotten Tomatoes based on 88 reviews. It earned five Academy Award nominations, including Best Supporting Actress for Gordon, whom it won, alongside nods for Best Screenplay and Best Art Direction. Commercially, the film grossed $33.4 million at the domestic box office on a $3.2 million budget, marking a significant return and contributing to the era's shift toward intelligent, character-driven horror over reliance on gore or monsters. Its influence persists in psychological thrillers exploring themes of bodily violation and institutional distrust, though the film's dream sequence depicting Rosemary's drugged assault drew censorship scrutiny in the UK, where 15 seconds were initially cut.
